parts.article:
The New Zealand writer Margaret Mahy
 
(A) In a career spanning some fifty years, Margaret Mahy has come to occupy a unique place in New Zealand writing with innovative fiction and original characterisation. In our solidly realist tradition, the linguistic fireworks of Mahy's children's fiction and the explorations of human behaviour at the heart of her supernatural teenage fiction stand gloriously alone. Mahy's clearest heir, I have always thought, is Elizabeth Knox — and maybe the true inheritance there is sheer singularity. Just as there is no one else like Knox in New Zealand writing, Mahy, too, has ventured into imaginative territory unknown to other local writers. So it was with great pleasure that I visited Mahy recently at her Governor's Bay home to talk about her new book. As with all journalists, she is generous to a fault with her time and attention; and, as always — despite her careful consideration of questions and thoughtful answers — I'm reminded she isn't truly comfortable making herself or her life the heart of any conversation.
 
(B) Certainly, any consideration of the style of Mahy's novels and picture books throws up some irresistible theories. As a writer committed to supporting herself through her art, she has seldom had the time for formal research. Rather, it has been a matter of going out and finding inspiration from her immediate environment: the writing on the side of a bus; a spelling mistake in a note to herself; the similarity between a cat and a fur hat. But despite these sometimes mundane origins, the settings for her stories are delightfully varied, as these books celebrate the dramatic plot twists and unpredictability of adventures on the high seas or in Antarctica, and also in quite unassuming places like the library or even down the back of a chair at home. Mahy has a lifelong affection for characters who are agents of upheaval and disturbance. Her junior and picture books are peppered with pirates, robbers and lions, though they appear alongside librarians, mothers and children, working against comfortable stereotype. Her fictions often have at their heart a young adult burdened with special powers, such as the ability to cast spells in order to transform their world in supernatural and fantastical ways. Another common feature is that, while the conclusions of her tales are usually predictable, they leave the reader feeling absolutely complete, the moral questions resulting from our hero's powers having been resolved.
 
(C) Many of these themes can be found in her new novel, The Magician of Hoad. The book was begun more than 15 years ago and envisioned as an 'entire' fantasy — one set in a fully imagined world with detailed history and complex tribal inter-relationships, a classical hero quest at its heart. The story ballooned at one point to 800 pages and has been through at least two substantial rewrites. Now half its original size, it is a fascinating read — an adventure, a romance, and a gold mine of Mahy literary preoccupations.
 
(D) The other splendid Mahy publication this year is a re-issue of Bubble Trouble in a now-illustrated edition. This tongue-twister tale first appeared in 1991, was included in 100 New Zealand Poems (1993) and has been recited by Mahy at countless private and public functions. Perhaps more than any other work, Bubble Trouble is the Mahy that New Zealand children and their parents know so well, the rollicking story of a clown who serves up a joyous torrent of word-play and unexpected rhyme.
 
(E) Those connections are four or five deep now. I read The Lion in the Meadow in the School Journal in the late 1960s; my step-daughter listened to The Boy Who Was Followed Home over and over in the 1970s; my own children sat very still mouthing The Great White Man-Eating Shark in the 80s and 90s; now, in the 21st century, my grandchildren have heard Down the Dragon's Tongue, A Summery Saturday Morning and Dashing Dog many times.
 
(F) Of course, readers are important to any working writer, but Mahy's espousal of the act of reading goes beyond that: a book is not properly finished, she has often said, until it has been read, because a reader brings something important to the book. So, doubtless out of need to build a market — she's not ignorant of her popularity — but also out of genuine care for that other dynamic part of the author-reader relationship, Mahy has, until recently, kept up a punishing schedule of public appearances.
 
(G) Private conversation with Mahy has always been a wild ride — marvellous, in the true sense of the word, the product of a hungry head and an infinite capacity to be astonished. She races away at one stage to consult an encyclopaedia for L. M. Montgomery's date of death, and speculates about the 'real' Montgomery, creator of the ever-popular Anne of Green Gables. Although I'd come to talk about her new book, I couldn't help but be captivated by her infectious curiosity.
 
(H) A few years ago, the writer David Hill told a funny story. Though his writing was, he conceded, very different from Mahy's, he had been affected by her peculiarly alert way of looking at the world, particularly the mad, slippery life of language. Once, Hill said, in a motel room, a sign on a door caught his eye: 'This door is alarmed.' Mahy would like that, thought Hill. She would enjoy the comedy just below the surface of the formal warning; she would leap immediately to the possibilities for story and language play: 'Yes, and this window is concerned, this light fitting is irritated.' His story was a wonderful comment on Mahy's vision.

Questions 27–31
Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 27–31 on your answer sheet, write:

Q27 Mahy explores the traditional themes of New Zealand literature.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q28 Mahy's children's books have been more popular than her teenage books.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q29 Mahy and Knox have sometimes criticised each other's work.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q30 Mahy is welcoming to interviewers.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q31 Mahy is at ease speaking about her experiences.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 32-35
Complete the summary below using the list of words and phrases A-I.
Write the correct letter A-I in boxes 32-35 on your answer sheet.
Theories about Mahy's style
Mahy's determination to earn a living from writing has encouraged her to find the ideas for her work in places. The stories themselves are set in locations that are . In terms of characterisation, almost all of her books feature unruly people, and very often an adolescent who possesses abilities. Finally, the endings of the stories tend to be .
  • A disruptive and unpredictable
  • B everyday
  • C loveable
  • D controversial
  • E exotic and ordinary
  • F isolated
  • G unconfident
  • H unsurprising but satisfying
  • I magical
Questions 36 – 40
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter A-D in boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet.

Q36 What does the writer say about The Magician of Hoad?

  • A It is partly based on true history.
  • B It was restructured in the writing process.
  • C It is quite different from conventional stories.
  • D It does not reflect the usual themes of Mahy's work.

Q37 According to the writer, Bubble Trouble

  • A was first illustrated in 1991.
  • B is written in plain language.
  • C is an old favourite for many families.
  • D has not been read aloud by Mahy before.

Q38 The writer's purpose in the fifth paragraph is to

  • A show how Mahy's style has changed through generations.
  • B criticise Mahy's children's stories for being repetitive.
  • C describe how new media have changed entertainment.
  • D illustrate Mahy's popularity with generations of children.

Q39 According to the sixth paragraph, which of the following is true?

  • A Readers sometimes do not finish Mahy's books.
  • B Mahy actively encourages feedback from readers.
  • C Readers are necessary in order to complete a book.
  • D Mahy does not realise how important she is to some readers.

Q40 What is the writer doing in the final paragraph?

  • A illustrating Mahy's view of the world
  • B comparing Mahy with another writer
  • C correcting a misconception about Mahy
  • D suggesting reasons for Mahy's approach

reference:
Q27

干扰 原文明确对比了“realist tradition”和Mahy的“stand alone / unknown territory”，说明她是非传统的。

句子 (Paragraph A) “In our solidly realist tradition... Mahy... has ventured into imaginative territory unknown to other local writers.”

解析 题目说Mahy探讨新西兰文学的传统主题。原文A段说新西兰文学是“solidly realist tradition（稳固的现实主义传统）”，而Mahy的作品是“innovative fiction（创新小说）”，并且她“ventured into imaginative territory unknown to other local writers（涉足了其他当地作家未知的想象领域）”，即她并未遵循传统主题，选 NO。

Q28

解析 题目说Mahy的儿童读物比她的青少年读物更受欢迎。原文A段虽然提到了这两种类型的书都“stand gloriously alone（独树一帜）”，但并没有比较两者的销量或受欢迎程度，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 不要因为自己更熟悉某种书就主观臆断，文中无比较级信息。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...Mahy's children's fiction and... her supernatural teenage fiction stand gloriously alone.” (No comparison)

Q29

解析 题目说Mahy和Knox有时互相批评对方的作品。原文A段作者认为Knox是Mahy的“heir（继承人）”，两人都有“sheer singularity（独特的奇特性）”，这是作者的评价，并未提到两人之间有过互动或批评，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 “Heir” 和 “no one else like...” 是赞赏性的比较，无关批评。

句子 (Paragraph A) “Mahy's clearest heir... is Elizabeth Knox... Just as there is no one else like Knox...”

Q30

句子 (Paragraph A) “As with all journalists, she is generous to a fault with her time and attention...”

解析 题目说Mahy对采访者很热情/欢迎。原文A段说对待所有记者，她都“generous to a fault with her time and attention（在时间和精力上极其慷慨）”，即非常欢迎，选 YES。

干扰 “Generous with time” 对应 “welcoming”。

Q31

解析 题目说Mahy在谈论自己的经历时感到自在（at ease）。原文A段末尾说她“isn't truly comfortable making herself or her life the heart of any conversation（把话题中心放在自己或生活上让她感到不自在）”，直接矛盾，选 NO。

干扰 “Not truly comfortable” 反驳了 “at ease”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...she isn't truly comfortable making herself or her life the heart of any conversation.”

Q32

解析 题目说她为了谋生，被迫从____地方寻找灵感。原文B段提到灵感来自“immediate environment（眼前环境）”，例如“writing on the side of a bus（公交车侧面的字）”等日常事物，对应选项 B (everyday)。

干扰 公交车、拼写错误、猫等都属于“everyday places/things”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...finding inspiration from her immediate environment: the writing on the side of a bus...”

Q33

解析 题目说故事背景设定在____的地点。原文B段提到地点既有“high seas or in Antarctica（公海或南极洲——exotic）”，也有“unassuming places like the library（图书馆——ordinary）”，对应选项 E。

干扰 原文用了“delightfully varied（令人愉快的变化多端）”来连接这两类截然不同的地点。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...adventures on the high seas or in Antarctica, and also in quite unassuming places like the library...”

Q34

干扰 “Cast spells / supernatural” 对应 “magical”。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...burdened with special powers, such as the ability to cast spells...”

解析 题目说青少年通常拥有____能力。原文B段提到年轻人拥有“special powers（特殊能力）”，例如“cast spells（施法）”来改变世界，对应选项 I (magical)。

Q35

解析 题目说故事结局往往是____。原文B段末尾说结局通常是“predictable（可预测的/unsurprising）”，但会让读者感到“absolutely complete（完全圆满/satisfying）”，对应选项 H。

干扰 需同时匹配两个形容词的含义。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...conclusions... are usually predictable, they leave the reader feeling absolutely complete...”

Q36

解析 题目问关于《The Magician of Hoad》作者说了什么。C段提到这本书曾经膨胀到800页，并经历了“at least two substantial rewrites（至少两次实质性重写）”，现在只有原来的一半大小，即写作过程中进行了重构，对应选项 B。

干扰 “Restructured” 对应 “rewrites / half its original size”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “The story ballooned... to 800 pages and has been through at least two substantial rewrites.”

Q37

句子 (Paragraph D) “...Bubble Trouble is the Mahy that New Zealand children and their parents know so well...”

解析 题目问关于《Bubble Trouble》。D段说这或许是新西兰孩子和父母最熟悉的Mahy作品（know so well），即它是许多家庭的老宠儿，对应选项 C。

干扰 A错在“first illustrated”，原文是“now-illustrated edition”（现在出了插图版），1991年是首次出版（first appeared）；D错在“not been read”，原文是“has been recited... at countless functions”。

Q38

解析 题目问第五段的目的是什么。E段作者列举了自己、继女、孩子到孙辈（generations）都在读Mahy的书，目的是展示她在几代孩子中的受欢迎程度，对应选项 D。

干扰 段落列举时间线（60s, 70s, 80s, 21st century）就是为了强调“generations”。

句子 (Paragraph E) 列举了四代人阅读Mahy作品的经历。

Q39

解析 题目问根据第六段哪项是正确的。F段提到Mahy认为书在被阅读之前不算真正完成，因为“a reader brings something important to the book”，即读者对完成一本书是必要的，对应选项 C。

干扰 “Necessary in order to complete” 对应 “not properly finished... until it has been read”。

句子 (Paragraph F) “...a book is not properly finished... until it has been read, because a reader brings something important...”

Q40

解析 题目问作者在最后一段在做什么。H段通过David Hill讲的关于“This door is alarmed”的故事，展示了Mahy独特的看待世界的方式（peculiarly alert way of looking at the world），对应选项 A（阐释Mahy的世界观）。

干扰 David Hill只是一个引子，目的是“comment on Mahy's vision（评论Mahy的视角）”。

句子 (Paragraph H) “His story was a wonderful comment on Mahy's vision.”
